title: Emergent Misalignment in Instruction-Tuned vs. Base Models: Does Chat Formatting Modulate the Effect?

original_idea.problem: Most EM experiments use instruction-tuned (chat) models. It is unclear whether base models — fine-tuned on raw completions — show the same EM signature, or whether instruction tuning is a prerequisite.
original_idea.direction: Select a model family with both a base and instruct variant at the same size (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). Fine-tune both on the same insecure-code dataset with matched hyperparameters. Evaluate both using the standard EM evaluation prompts (reformatted appropriately for base models). Compare misalignment rates.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: The core finding (base models show EM, potentially more than instruct models) already exists in the original paper. A more controlled replication adds modest value.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires fine-tuning two model variants with matched hyperparameters and adapting evaluation prompts for base models. A beginner CS student would need guidance on SFT pipelines and evaluation design, but existing EM codebases provide a starting point. The base-model evaluation reformatting adds non-trivial complexity.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-bounded: two fine-tuning runs, one evaluation comparison. The first deliverable (misalignment rate comparison between base and instruct variants) is clear and standalone. Feasible in 30hrs with LoRA on a single GPU.

novelty.reasoning: The original Betley et al. paper included a finding that 'models finetuned from the base model show higher rates of misaligned answers than models finetuned from the instruct-tuned model,' which directly addresses this idea's core hypothesis. However, this was not the paper's primary focus and was tested in a limited setting. The idea proposes a more controlled comparison with matched hyperparameters on a specific model family (Llama-3.2-3B). The question of whether instruction tuning is a prerequisite for EM has a preliminary answer (no, base models show it too, even more so), but a systematic characterization with matched conditions and evaluation prompt reformatting for base models has room for additional work. The core finding already exists, reducing novelty.

evidence: Betley et al. (2025). Emergent Misalignment. arXiv:2502.17424. Tested base vs. instruct variants.
Nature (2026). Training large language models on narrow tasks can lead to broad misalignment.
